title: Gas Exchange in Plants
notes: Green plants make their own food by **photosynthesis**, which uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. They also **respire** all the time, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. The gases you can detect around a leaf depend on which process is faster, so the **net gas exchange** is not fixed: it changes with light.

In bright light both processes run, but photosynthesis is faster. The leaf therefore uses more carbon dioxide than it produces and releases more oxygen than it uses. You see a **net uptake of carbon dioxide** and a **net release of oxygen**. For example, a leaf in hydrogencarbonate indicator turns it from red to purple, because the carbon dioxide level drops below normal.

In darkness photosynthesis stops but respiration continues. The plant now takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide, so there is a **net release of carbon dioxide** and a **net uptake of oxygen**. The gases move through tiny pores called **stomata** on the leaf surface. Respiration never stops, even in bright light — it is only hidden by the faster photosynthesis.
callout: Do not write that plants respire only at night — respiration runs all the time; light just lets photosynthesis overtake it.

questions.prompt: A green plant is left in bright sunlight. Which row describes its net gas exchange?

options.text: Net uptake of carbon dioxide and net release of oxygen
Net release of carbon dioxide and net uptake of oxygen
Net uptake of both carbon dioxide and oxygen
No net exchange, because the two processes cancel out

questions.why: Photosynthesis runs faster than respiration in bright light, so the plant takes in more carbon dioxide than it makes and gives out more oxygen than it uses.
questions.wrongWhy: Both processes run, but photosynthesis is faster, so they do not cancel out. Answer: net uptake of carbon dioxide and net release of oxygen.

questions.prompt: A leaf is sealed in a tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator that is red at the start. After five hours in bright light the indicator is purple. What does this show?

options.text: The leaf released carbon dioxide faster than it used it
The leaf used up more carbon dioxide than it released
The leaf stopped respiring in the light
The indicator changed colour because of the light itself

questions.why: Purple means the carbon dioxide level has fallen below normal, so photosynthesis removed more carbon dioxide than respiration added.
questions.wrongWhy: Purple marks a fall in carbon dioxide, not a rise, and light alone does not change the indicator. Answer: the leaf used up more carbon dioxide than it released.

questions.prompt: A potted plant is sealed in a clear box overnight in the dark. What happens to the air inside the box?

options.text: Carbon dioxide falls and oxygen rises
Carbon dioxide rises and oxygen falls
Both gases stay at the same level
Oxygen rises because the plant stops respiring

questions.why: In darkness only respiration occurs, so the plant takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
questions.wrongWhy: The plant does not stop respiring at night — respiration continues without photosynthesis. Answer: carbon dioxide rises and oxygen falls.

questions.prompt: Through which leaf structure do carbon dioxide and oxygen mainly enter and leave?
questions.why: Stomata are the pores on the leaf surface that let carbon dioxide and oxygen move in and out.
questions.wrongWhy: Guard cells sit around each stoma and control its opening, but the gases pass through the pore itself. Answer: stomata.
